## What this document is

A runnable version of the Session 0 guide. Every claim below is executed, not
asserted — which is the harness's own discipline applied to my notes about it.

Render it from the `prove-it` directory:

```sh
quarto render lab/docs/session-0.qmd   # this page
quarto render lab/docs                 # the whole site
quarto preview lab/docs                # live reload while writing
```

The source lives in `lab/docs/`, but `_quarto.yml` sets
`opts_knit: root.dir: "../.."`, so chunks execute two levels up in `prove-it/`.
That is why every command below reads exactly as it does in the session
guides — no `../`, no `cd`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading exit codes

Half of this document is about commands that fail **on purpose**. A test that
goes red, a gate that refuses. So chunks use this pattern throughout:

```bash
some-command > /dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?
echo "exit=$rc"
```

The redirect keeps the transcript readable, `rc=$?` captures the status before
anything clobbers it, and the final `echo` lets the chunk itself succeed so the
render continues. `0` means success; anything else is a failure.
:::

## Start from a known state

Every chunk below assumes no leftover runs. This makes the document
idempotent — render it as many times as you like.

```{bash}
find runs -mindepth 1 ! -name .gitkeep -delete 2>/dev/null
find control/receipts -name '*.json' -delete 2>/dev/null
cp control/checks/fixtures/solution-stub.mjs working/src/slugify.mjs
echo "reset: no runs, no receipts, candidate restored to the broken stub"
```

---

## The idea in one paragraph

An agent writes the code, writes the test, runs the test, reads the output, and
reports the result. Every link in the evidence chain routes through the party
being judged. `prove-it` answers that with a split enforced by directory:
`working/` is the only place worker tools can write, and `control/` is
host-owned — the gate, its signing key, the contracts, the receipts.

A run completes only when `dr-gate` reruns the agreed checks **itself** and
signs a receipt. Everything that follows is an elaboration of that sentence.

---

## Task 1 — Readiness

The first question is whether the course runs on this machine at all. Every row
of this script is an actual attempt: it really reads the Node version, really
writes into `runs/`, really looks for a provider CLI on `PATH`.


```{bash}
bash sessions/s0-setup/fixtures/readiness.sh
```

Required rows must say `READY`. The `claude` and `codex` rows may say `ABSENT` —
the required path is keyless and offline.

## Task 2 — The green check

This drives the entire workflow once, in a throwaway copy under `/tmp`, and
asserts eight things along the way. It never touches this checkout, so it can be
run at any time without cleaning up first.

```{bash}
bash scripts/green-check.sh
```

The eight assertions in four groups:

| Group | Asserts |
|---|---|
| Is the task real? | the stub fails; the agent completes its turns; the check then passes |
| Does the evidence path work? | the gate issues a receipt; completion consumes it |
| Does the gate refuse? | a forged signature is rejected; a stale tree is rejected |
| Is the contract sound? | the shipped contract parses and is accepted |

Two details worth noticing in the source. The forgery and staleness assertions
don't merely check for a non-zero exit — they grep for the *exact* refusal
string, so the test can't pass because the gate crashed on a typo. And the
script deliberately declines to test OS containment, saying so in its own
footer. That question gets its own section below.

---

## The loop, one step at a time

```
contract  →  open  →  work  →  dr-gate check  →  complete
```

### The contract

The loop does not start with work. It starts with a written definition of done,
frozen before anyone touches anything.

```{bash}
cat done/contract.yaml
```

Eight keys — and they are **not** equal in force. Only some are enforced by the
gate; the rest are prose for humans:

| Enforced by the gate | Declarative only |
|---|---|
| `checks` — rerun, exit code compared | `outcome` |
| `protect` — hashed at open, re-verified | `runtime_observation` |
| the contract's own sha256 | `must_change` / `must_not_change` |
| | `budgets`, `stop_and_ask`, `release_owner` |

`must_not_change` really is in the right-hand column. Proof:

```{bash}
gate=$(grep -c "must_not_change" control/dr-gate.ts)
parser=$(grep -c "must_not_change" src/contract.ts)
echo "must_not_change in src/contract.ts (parsed): $parser"
echo "must_not_change in control/dr-gate.ts (enforced): $gate"
```

It reads like a guarantee and functions as a comment. What actually protects the
fixture's test file is a host-owned manifest:

```{bash}
cat control/checks/manifest.json
```

That distinction is the single most important thing to carry into my own
contract, where there is no manifest and `protect:` is the only mechanism with
teeth.

### `open` — freeze the identities

`open` does no work. It records what is about to be judged.

```{bash}
node src/loop.ts open --run-id demo
echo "---"
cat runs/demo/run.json
```

The rule: **the definition and the yardstick are frozen; the thing being
measured is free to move.** `contract_sha256` must not change — moving it is
moving the goalposts. `candidate_tree_start` is expected to change, because
changing it is the work.

(`candidate_tree_start` is recorded and then never read by the gate. It is
provenance, not a constraint. The tree hash that can refuse you is a different
one, taken later at `check`.)

### The candidate starts red

The shipped `slugify.mjs` throws. This is deliberate: a check that has never
been seen failing is not a check.

```{bash}
node --test working/test/slugify.test.mjs 2>&1 | tail -6
```

```{bash}
node --test working/test/slugify.test.mjs > /dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?
echo "exit=$rc"
```

### The worker works

`--provider smoke` is a scripted fake agent — no API key, no network, the same
code path a real provider would take.

```{bash}
node src/loop.ts run --provider smoke --run-id first
```

It read the file, wrote an implementation, ran the check, failed, wrote again,
and passed. Its closing line is a claim of completion.

The status is `needs_evidence`.

### The claim buys nothing

The code works and the test passes. Claim the run is done.

```{bash}
node src/loop.ts complete first; rc=$?
echo "exit=$rc"
```

`complete` forms no opinion of its own. It shells out to the gate and asks a
single question — *is there a valid receipt?* — and there isn't. The word
`completed` cannot be written by anything on the worker's side of the house.

### `dr-gate check` — the judgment

The gate re-reads the contract and confirms its hash still matches what `open`
pinned, verifies the protected test file is untouched, hashes the candidate
tree, then **runs the check command itself** in a fresh subprocess and compares
the exit code. Only then does it sign.

```{bash}
node control/dr-gate.ts check first
```

### The receipt

```{bash}
cat control/receipts/first.json
```

Four identities, the check results, and one signature:

- `contract_sha256` — which definition of done
- `check_version` — which checks
- `candidate_tree` — which exact bytes of code
- `run_id` — which run (this is what defeats replay)
- `sig` — an HMAC keyed with `control/gate.key`, which the worker cannot read

Every field is reconstructible from worker context **except** `sig`. That is the
whole security argument.

The receipt asserts exactly this:

> These named checks, run by the gate itself, against this exact tree, with
> these protected files byte-identical to `open`, under these exact contract
> bytes, produced these exit codes.

It does **not** assert that the checks were adequate.

### `complete` — now it lands

```{bash}
node src/loop.ts complete first
```

---

## Three refusals

A gate is worth exactly what it refuses.

### 1. A forged signature

Every field is genuine except `sig`.

```{bash}
node --input-type=module -e "
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
const p = 'control/receipts/first.json';
const j = JSON.parse(readFileSync(p, 'utf8'));
const s = j.sig;
j.sig = s.slice(0, -1) + (s.slice(-1) === 'a' ? 'b' : 'a');
writeFileSync(p, JSON.stringify(j, null, 2));
console.log('flipped one hex character of sig');
"
node control/dr-gate.ts verify first; rc=$?
echo "exit=$rc"
```

### 2. A stale candidate

Re-sign, then change the code *after* the receipt was issued.

```{bash}
node control/dr-gate.ts check first | head -1
echo "--- now edit the checked file ---"
echo "// drift" >> working/src/slugify.mjs
node control/dr-gate.ts verify first; rc=$?
echo "exit=$rc"
```

The receipt still describes code that no longer exists.

### 3. A moved contract

```{bash}
git checkout -- working/src/slugify.mjs
node src/loop.ts open --run-id goalpost
echo "# small clarifying tweak" >> done/contract.yaml
node control/dr-gate.ts check goalpost; rc=$?
echo "exit=$rc"
git checkout -- done/contract.yaml
echo "(contract restored)"
```

Three attacks, three *different* refusal reasons. The gate names which pin
broke rather than failing generically.

A fourth is worth knowing without running it: copy a valid receipt onto another
run and the signature still verifies perfectly — the payload is genuine — but
`run_id` doesn't match, so it refuses with `receipt run mismatch`. **A true
receipt can still be the wrong receipt.**

---

## What is *not* protected

Everything above is enforced by the harness's own tool layer. Whether the
operating system would stop a determined process is a separate question, and the
probe answers it honestly.

```{bash}
bash scripts/probe.sh
```

Four of six actions are refused by tool-layer *policy*. Zero are contained by
the OS. A policy refusal is not a sandbox, and the footer says so in as many
words.

---

## Adequacy is not provenance

The gate is rigorous about where a result came from and completely indifferent
to whether the check was worth running. The course ships a deliberately weak
contract to make the point:

```{bash}
cat sessions/s1-define-done/fixtures/weak-contract.yaml
```

Schema-complete — every required key present. It would pass any structural
validation. Now run its two checks against the **untouched broken stub**:

```{bash}
cp control/checks/fixtures/solution-stub.mjs working/src/slugify.mjs

echo -n "the real test:      "
node --test working/test/slugify.test.mjs > /dev/null 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"

echo -n "weak check 1:       "
node -e "import('./working/src/slugify.mjs').then(() => process.exit(0))" 2>/dev/null; echo "exit=$?"

echo -n "weak check 2:       "
bash -c 'node --test working/test/slugify.test.mjs || echo done anyway' > /dev/null 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"
```

Both of the weak contract's checks are green against code that is definitively
broken. The exploit is not "cut corners" — it is **do nothing at all** and
collect a valid signed receipt.

They fail differently, and the distinction matters:

- **Check 1 is vacuous.** It imports the module and never calls the function.
  Nothing is suppressed; it runs honestly and exits 0 honestly. It proves the
  file is syntactically valid JavaScript and nothing more.
- **Check 2 is suppressed.** The real test runs and genuinely fails, and
  `|| echo done anyway` discards the exit code. The failure output is still
  printed, and still written to `check-output.txt` — legible to any human,
  invisible to every mechanism in the system.

The gate does defend against suppression, with a blocklist:

```{bash}
sed -n '14p' control/dr-gate.ts
```

Check `|| echo done anyway` against that list. It is not `|| true`. It is not a
trailing `exit 0`. **It sails straight through.** A blocklist stops the
suppression you thought of.

::: {.callout-important}
## The habit this buys

**Run every check against known-broken code and watch it go red before trusting
it.** A check never seen failing is not a check — it is a command that happens
to exit 0, and reading it cannot tell you which. Check 1 looks entirely
reasonable on the page and is inert.
:::

## What carries forward

1. **The worker's "done" is an opinion.** Only a gate-verified receipt changes a
   run's status.
2. **A receipt binds provenance, not quality.** Which contract, which checks,
   which bytes — never whether the checks were the right ones.
3. **`protect` has teeth; `must_not_change` is a comment.** On my own repo there
   is no manifest, so `protect:` is the only real mechanism.
4. **A check never seen red is not a check.**
5. **Policy refusal is not containment.** Zero of six, on this host.
